doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Supportive parents and learning clarinet in the Bronx
summary: Parents supported his music; clarinet in fourth grade, practicing little, becoming second best, Benny Goodman as first hero in Parkchester.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Were your parents supportive of a career in music?

My dad was funny. He was in the printing business with a couple of his brothers. And once in a while he’d say, when I was listening to Benny Goodman, my first hero, and he’d go like this, “You blow that thing.” And he would forget it was a clarinet or something. But they were good. They got me a silver clarinet when I first started. I made the music class in the fourth grade. And the funny thing was they played for about 40 of us. There was a piano and the teacher said, “Okay kids. Is this the same note?” [scats] “Or a different note?” [scats] And a lot of kids got it wrong. I’m laughing but I got it right. That’s all I remember from the test. So I was in the fifth and sixth grade music class. Mostly violinists. There was about 40 kids. And I played clarinet. And the first year literally I was the worst clarinet player because I was this tiny little kid that loved to play basketball. So when I played my clarinet, I practiced 20 minutes a day. Now it takes 5 minutes to put the horn together with the cork grease and everything, and 5 minutes to put it away. And I want to go out and put on my sneakers and play. So I probably played 15 minutes, 10 or 15 minutes. But at the end of the year the clarinet teacher that came in, he wasn’t the teacher there, he came in a private room in the back. He’d teach about 10 of us. But when you’re in the fifth grade, a little tiny kid, there are these twins and when we played, you’d play a tune like “Lightly Row” so we’d play like this [scats]. You take a breath for every note. It was cute when I think about it now. So they’d make me laugh, looking at other kids, and I was probably the worst. But the teacher would get us in front of our regular teacher, our homeroom teacher, who was a piano player, a very sweet lady, and we’d play for the rest of the class. Twenty violinists and one or two viola players or whatever. And we’d stand up there and challenge each other. We’d play some tune. And the clarinet teacher would pick who was the best. So at the end of the semester he wrote in my yearbook, “Practice more.” It was cute you know. And for some reason, I really don’t remember, I started to practice more, and I became about the second best clarinetist in the class. And I remember hearing people in the project where I lived, in Parkchester in

the Bronx, thousands of kids. And there were a couple of kids that played, they were playing sort of Benny Goodman tunes, I mean much better than me. I could barely play anything improvising. I was listening to Benny Goodman, my first hero, and trying to copy a couple of licks. I didn’t have any ear, I could play a couple of licks and I felt great. I mean three or four licks, that was it. But as a little kid you feel wonderful that you can do anything. Or play a tune, “Sing, Sing, Sing” you know. But I remember some kids, I started to pass them as I got the next year or two or three you know. They weren’t so great anymore you know. I remember my brother’s friend was playing “Tenderly” on alto when I first started playing alto, a couple of years later, after the clarinet. And if I could even play the melody, forget about intonation or anything, you know.
